questions.q: Which of these is listed as a tourism and hospitality higher education institution in Oman?

questions.q: Which institution is NOT on the slides' list of T&H education providers in Oman?

questions.q: Under Oman's Tanfeedh plan, which sectors are targeted for development alongside tourism?
questions.d: Tourism, industrial and logistics sectors are targeted under Tanfeedh for economic diversification.
questions.w: The government wants new jobs in these sectors prioritised for Omanis.

questions.q: How many jobs are predicted to be created by Oman Tourism Strategy 2016–2040?
questions.d: Job opportunities: more than 500,000 jobs predicted from the strategy.
questions.w: 11 million is the tourist target, not jobs.

questions.q: About how many DIRECT tourism jobs are forecast by 2040?
questions.d: Direct jobs by 2040: about 321,863.
questions.w: 73,224 is the hospitality share; 137,000 is diploma-to-bachelor jobs.

questions.q: What share of direct tourism jobs in 2040 will be in the hospitality sector?
questions.d: Hospitality: 22.75% (73,224); other tourism-related sectors: 77.25% (248,639).
questions.w: Most direct jobs are outside hospitality.

questions.q: Overall Omanization in tourism jobs by 2040 is expected to be around:
questions.d: Omanization: around 70% overall; around 90% in managerial and middle-management positions.
questions.w: 90% applies to managerial positions only.

questions.q: Omanization in managerial and middle-management tourism positions is expected to be around:
questions.d: Managerial and middle-management Omanization: about 90%.
questions.w: The overall figure is 70%.

questions.q: Jobs requiring a diploma, advanced diploma or bachelor's degree are expected to be about:
questions.d: Diploma, advanced diploma and bachelor jobs: around 137,000, about 61% of total jobs.
questions.w: This shows the value of tourism education.

questions.q: Most of the new tourism jobs will be in the:
questions.d: Job opportunities: most jobs will be in the private sector.
questions.w: Hotels, transport and tour companies are mostly private businesses.

questions.q: Directors and managers who lead and supervise an area, programme or project are at the:
questions.d: Job levels (2040): superior (directors, managers), medium technical (specialised and skilled), basic (wage-earning manual work).
questions.w: Leadership positions are superior level.

questions.q: Positions needing theoretical and conceptual knowledge of a specialisation, plus technical or skilled support roles, are at the:
questions.d: Medium technical level: specialised knowledge and support, operational, technical, skilled or semi-skilled positions.
questions.w: It sits between managers and manual work.

questions.q: Wage-earning jobs, especially manual-labour and industrial work, are at the:
questions.d: Basic level: positions employed for wages, mainly manual and skilled labour.
questions.w: Manual work is basic level.

questions.q: Working for a travel agent or tour operator is employment in the:
questions.d: Tourism suppliers: transportation, accommodation, F&B, attractions, sales distribution (travel agents, tour operators), events.
questions.w: Travel agents and tour operators sell tourism products.

questions.q: Forts, museums, the opera house and protected areas offer jobs in the:
questions.d: Attractions: forts, museums, opera house, protected areas.
questions.w: These are places tourists visit.

questions.q: Starting your own tourism or hospitality business is called:
questions.d: Tourism entrepreneurship: establishing a business in the tourism and hospitality industry.
questions.w: Creating your own business is entrepreneurship.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a HOSPITALITY career on the slides?
questions.d: Hospitality careers: hotel/resort, restaurant, front office, housekeeping, F&B, banquet, events, guest relations managers, etc.
questions.w: The other options are listed as tourism careers.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a TOURISM career on the slides?
questions.d: Tourism careers: tour guide, tour manager, tourism officer, travel agency manager, ticketing manager, airline ground staff, travel consultant, museum manager, etc.
questions.w: The other options are hospitality careers.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the soft skills listed for working in tourism and hospitality?
questions.d: Soft skills: patience, communication, customer service, outgoing and enthusiastic, multitasking, problem-solving, teamwork, adaptability, stress and time management, professionalism.

o: No two days are the same, and you meet new people

You can work anywhere in the world
Part-time jobs are easy to find

questions.d: Positive sides: tourism creates many jobs, about one job in ten.

questions.q: Internships, training, student clubs and volunteering belong to which career planning step?

questions.q: Outline the sectors and organisations that offer jobs to tourism and hospitality graduates.
questions.a:
1. National Tourism Organisations: Oman Ministry of Heritage and Tourism.
2. Tourism suppliers: transportation (airports, airlines, car rentals, ports, bus companies); accommodation (hotels, motels, apartments, camps, heritage inns); F&B (restaurants, coffee shops); attractions (forts, museums, opera house, protected areas); sales distribution (travel agents, tour operators); events (Oman Convention and Exhibition Centre, festivals).
3. Other government organisations: OMRAN, Oman Airports Management Company, Royal Oman Police, Royal Court, ministries, embassies.
4. International organisations: GCC, Arab Tourism Organisation, UNWTO.
5. Tourism entrepreneurship: your own business.
questions.d: Where to work: the employers available to tourism and hospitality graduates.
questions.w: Group the employers into these five categories.

questions.q: Discuss the positive and negative sides of working in tourism and hospitality.
questions.a:
Positive:
- One of the largest and fastest-growing industries; about 1 in 10 jobs.
- Many tourism projects in Oman, so more job opportunities.
- Easy entry; jobs for all ages, even without experience.
- Transferable skills, so you can work anywhere; faster promotion.
- Excellent work environment (hotels, resorts, airports); no two days the same; meeting new people.
- Easy part-time work; good salaries for top positions.
Negative:
- Long hours, especially in peak season; 24/365 operations; working holidays and night shifts.
- High turnover; negative public perception.
- More part-time and casual workers; low entry-level pay.
- Seasonal and informal jobs; competition from unskilled labour; labour moving between sectors.
questions.d: Working in tourism and hospitality has both advantages and challenges.
questions.w: Balance the answer with several points on each side.

questions.q: Outline the main steps for career planning in tourism and hospitality.
questions.a:
1. Conduct a self-assessment and know yourself.
2. Learn about the careers that suit you.
3. Explore and visit the organisations you would like to work in.
4. Understand the attributes, skills and knowledge required.
5. Engage in networking.
6. Gain work experience (internships, training, students' clubs, volunteering).
questions.d: Career planning: a step-by-step process for choosing and preparing for a career.
questions.w: The steps move from knowing yourself to gaining real experience.
